title: Excellence in everything
hookLine: Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, even sharpening the blade to spare the animal (Nawawi 17, Shaddad ibn Aws)
tomorrow: you messed up. what do you do in the next five minutes?

cards: Why does a hadith about excellence mention sharpening a blade? Every job has two speeds: fast enough for the line, or good enough for the cup. The essay at midnight.
The dishes. The bathroom cleaned when nobody's coming over. A text sent, or a text read over once before sending.

Al-Nawawi's seventeenth hadith settles which speed counts by choosing a hard example on purpose: the moment an animal is slaughtered for food. A gentle note for younger listeners: it's about sparing the animal pain.

teach.b: From Sahih Muslim, told by Shaddad ibn Aws, in paraphrase: Allah has prescribed ihsan in everything. So when you slaughter, slaughter well: let each of you sharpen his blade, and spare the animal suffering.
Ihsan is doing a thing well, all the way through; you met the same word in the stranger in white. And here two readings speak.
The first says: it's craft. In everything means everything: the cup, the essay, the bed. Do the ordinary thing as well as it can be done, because it's done before Allah.
That's the barista who wipes the steam wand every single time, though no customer would ever know. A dull blade is a skill problem, and sloppiness is its own unkindness.
The second says: it's mercy. Look at the example the hadith picks.
Not a beautiful product, but a creature's last moment. The blade is sharpened so the animal suffers less.

Excellence is measured by what it spares the one on the receiving end, and polish for its own sake can turn into vanity. That's the nurse who warms her hands before touching a patient. Neither reading drops the other.
The craft camp sharpens for the animal's sake too. The mercy camp still sharpens.

how: Muslims who slaughter for food, at Eid al-Adha or at the butcher's, sharpen the blade beforehand and keep it out of the animal's sight, citing this hadith; teachers also use it for doing ordinary work well.

practice: Take a pen and write one word by hand, your name or today's line, slowly, as well as you can make it. No speed, no audience. If your hand wants to rush, notice it, then slow it again.
Then rest your eyes on it for the remainder of the sit, a small thing done all the way.

wordCard.voice: Ihsan: doing it well, all the way through, in everything, from the cup to the blade. Today's hadith puts the word in its very first line.

orig.note: Arabic: excellence, doing a thing well; the word in the hadith's first line.

carryVoice: Keep this one: even the blade, where done well and done kindly turn out to be the same task. Hadith seventeen, sharpened.
